title: Manners and paying a visit
goal: Get through a visit to a Javanese home from the door to saying goodbye — what is said, in what order, and the things done with the body rather than the mouth.
bekal: opening the conversation at the door with *kula nuwun* and answering *mangga*
following the order of a visit: entering, sitting, being served, taking leave
recognizing body manners: hands, where to walk, how to point

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sowan menyang omahé simbahé Rini
dialogs.intro: Dian goes home to Klaten with Rini. It is her first visit to a truly traditional Javanese home, and the whole conversation is in krama. Notice the order — it is almost always the same anywhere in Java.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Hello, may I come in?… (at the door)

lines.speaker: Simbah:
lines.id: Please, come on in. Who's this?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: My friend, Mbah. Her name is Dian.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Sugeng sonten, Mbah. Nami kula Dian.
lines.id: Good afternoon, Mbah. My name is Dian.
lines.literal: good afternoon, Grandma. name my Dian.

lines.speaker: Simbah:
lines.id: Please sit down. Where are you from, dear?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Saking Jakarta, Mbah. Kula kuliah wonten Ngayogya.
lines.id: From Jakarta, Mbah. I'm studying in Yogyakarta.
lines.literal: from Jakarta, Grandma. I study at Yogyakarta.

lines.speaker: Simbah:
lines.id: Oh, that's far. Please, have your drink.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: I have, Mbah. Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Mbah, kula kaliyan Dian badhé kondur rumiyin, nggih.
lines.id: Mbah, Dian and I are going to head home now.
lines.literal: Grandma, I with Dian going-to go-home first, yes.

lines.speaker: Simbah:
lines.text: Nggih, ngatos-atos. Mbénjing mriki malih, nggih.
lines.id: All right, take care. Come here again some time.
lines.literal: yes, careful. later here again, yes.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Inggih, Mbah. Nyuwun pamit. Sugeng kantun.
lines.id: Yes, Mbah. We'll take our leave. Goodbye.
lines.literal: yes, Grandma. beg leave. well staying.

notes: **Kula nuwun** is said **at the door**, before going in — the spoken equivalent of knocking, and often said while knocking. The answer is always *mangga*. The ngoko form is just *nuwun*, and in many areas people say *assalamualaikum* instead.

**Nduk** is an affectionate way to address a girl, from *gendhuk*. Its partner is *Lé*, from *thulé*, for a boy. Older people use them for anyone much younger, and hearing it is a sign you have been accepted, not looked down on.

**Wédangipun dipun-unjuk** — notice that the host offers with a **passive** sentence rather than a direct command. This is where the patterns of units 12 and 18 meet: a command to a respected person is wrapped in the passive so it doesn't sound like a command.
**Sampun dhahar dèrèng? Wonten sekul.** — An offer of food is almost certain to come. If you answer *dèrèng* (not yet), food really will be prepared, so answer according to what you actually want.

**Nyuwun pamit** is the formal way of taking leave, and it is **required** — leaving a Javanese home without a spoken goodbye is one of the few things considered truly rude. The ngoko form is *aku pamit dhisik*.
**Mbénjing mriki malih** — "come here again some time". This isn't an invitation you need to schedule; it is a natural closing, like "come and see us again" in English.

grammars.title: The order of a visit, and what to say at each stage
body: A visit to a Javanese home has an almost fixed order. Learning the sentences for each stage lets you get through the whole visit without having to build sentences yourself.
after: **The three must-say sentences**: *kula nuwun* at the door, *matur nuwun* when served, *nyuwun pamit* when leaving. Say those three and the whole visit will feel right, even if you answer everything else in a simpler language.

**Don't take your leave as soon as the refreshments are finished.** Waiting a few minutes afterward is a habit people notice. Leaving the moment your glass is empty reads as if you only came for the drink.

blocks.text: Most Javanese politeness is never spoken. Here are the things people notice without ever mentioning them, and all are easy once you know.

items: **Passing in front of older people**: bend forward a little, lower your right hand ahead of you, and say *nuwun sèwu*. In its most formal version this is called **laku dhodhok**; in daily life a slight bow is enough.
**Give and receive with the right hand**. Use the left hand only if you must, and then say *nuwun sèwu*. Handing something over with both hands is even more respectful.

**Point with your thumb**, not your index finger. The index finger is for pointing at objects, and even then some people still use the thumb. Pointing at a person with your index finger reads as rude.
**Sit lower than the person you respect**, if possible. If they sit on a chair and you sit on the floor, that is no insult to you — it is the normal arrangement.

**Shaking hands**: shaking an older person's hand is often followed by bringing the back of their hand toward your forehead or nose. This is called **salim**, and it is a common sign of respect, not only within the family.
**Sungkem** — kneeling and kissing an elder's knee or hand — is done on special occasions: Lebaran, weddings, before a long journey. As a guest you aren't expected to do it, but you will see it.

blocks.title: Four things best avoided
items: **Standing with your hands on your hips** while talking to an older person. It reads as a challenge.
**Crossing your legs high** in front of elders or in a traditional front room.
**Refusing refreshments entirely** with no reason. Take a little; that is enough.
**Speaking loudly and fast.** Spoken Javanese is slow and even. A loud voice reads as anger, even if your words are polite.

blocks.title: Nyuwun pangapunten: an apology with weight
items: *Nyuwun pangapunten* is a real apology, used for an actual mistake. For an everyday "excuse me", use *nuwun sèwu*.
Mixing them up does no harm, but using *nyuwun pangapunten* for something small sounds overdone — like bowing deeply for spilling a little water.

Around Lebaran the full form becomes *nyuwun pangapunten lahir batos* — please forgive me, inside and out. You will get it by text from nearly everyone you know, and replying with the same sentence is enough.
